source_text: Si de exomologesi retractas, gehennam in corde considera, quam tibi exomologesis extinguet, et poenae prius magnitudinem imaginare, ut de remedii adoptione non dubites. Quid illum thesaurum ignis aeterni aestimamus, cum fumariola quaedam eius tales flammarum ictus suscitent, ut proximae urbes aut iam nullae extent aut idem sibi de die sperent? Dissiliunt superbissimi montes ignis intrinsecus fetu, et quod nobis iudicii perpetuitatem probat, cum dissiliant, cum devorentur, nunquam tamen finiuntur. Quis haec supplicia interim montium non iudicii minantis exemplaria deputabit? quis scintillas tales non magni alicuius et inaestimabilis foci missilia quaedam et exercitoria iacula consentiet? Igitur cum scias adversus gehennam post prima illa intinctionis dominicae munimenta esse adhuc in exomologesi secunda subsidia, cur salutem tuam deseris? cur cessas aggredi quod scias mederi tibi? Mutae quidem animae et irrationales medicinas sibi divinitus attributas in tempore agnoscunt. Cervus sagitta transfixus, ut ferrum et irrevocabiles moras eius de vulnere expellat, scit sibi dictamno medendum. Hirundo, si excaecaverit pullos, novit illos oculare rursus de sua chelidonia. Peccator restituendo sibi institutam a domino exomologesin sciens praeteribit illam, quae Babylonium regem in regna restituit? Diu enim paenitentiam domino immolarat, septenni squalore exomologesin operatus, unguium aquilinum in modum efferatione et capilli incuria horrorem leoninum praeferente. Proh malae tractationis! Quem homines perhorrebant, deus recipiebat. Contra autem Aegyptius imperator, qui populum dei aliquando afflictum, diu domino suo denegatum, persecutus in proelium irruit, post tot documenta plagarum discidio maris, quod soli populo pervium licebat, revolutis fluctibus periit. Paenitentiam enim et ministerium eius exomologesin abiecerat. Quid ego ultra de istis duabus humanae salutis quasi plancis, stili potius negotium quam officium conscientiae meae curans? Peccator enim omnium notarum cum sim, nec ulli rei nisi paenitentiae natus, non facile possum super illa tacere, quam ipse quoque et stirpis humanae et offensae in dominum princeps Adam, exomologesi restitutus in paradisum suum, non tacet.
thought_title: The remedy of public confession against hell
orientation: Tertullian is urging the sinner not to shrink from public confession by picturing the eternal fire it extinguishes and by examples from nature and Scripture.
pass_a_gloss: If you shrink back from public confession, consider hell in your heart, which public confession will extinguish for you, and first imagine the greatness of the punishment, so that you may not doubt about adopting the remedy. What do we think that treasure of eternal fire is, when certain little smoke-vents of it stir up such strikes of flames that nearby cities either no longer exist or hope for the same for themselves from day to day? The proudest mountains burst apart from the offspring of fire within, and what proves to us the endlessness of judgment, when they burst apart, when they are devoured, they are never finished. Who will not reckon these punishments of mountains for the time being as examples of a threatening judgment? Who will not agree that such sparks are certain missiles and practice darts of some great and incalculable furnace? Therefore, since you know that against hell, after those first defenses of the Lord's baptism, there are still second aids in public confession, why do you abandon your salvation? Why do you stop undertaking what you know heals you? Dumb and irrational souls indeed recognize in time the medicines divinely assigned to them. A deer pierced by an arrow, so that it may expel the iron and its irrevocable delays from the wound, knows that it must be healed by dittany. A swallow, if it has blinded its chicks, knows how to give them sight again from its own celandine. Will the sinner, knowing that public confession was instituted for him by the Lord for restoring him, pass over that which restored the Babylonian king to his kingdom? For he had long sacrificed repentance to the Lord, having worked public confession in seven-year squalor, with the wildness of his nails in the manner of an eagle's talons and the neglect of his hair presenting a lion-like horror. Alas for the harsh treatment! The man whom humans shuddered at, God was receiving. On the other hand, the Egyptian ruler, who had pursued the people of God, once afflicted, long denied to their Lord, and rushed into battle, perished after so many proofs of plagues, when the sea parted, which was passable for the people alone, and the waves rolled back. For he had cast away repentance and its ministry, public confession. Why should I go further about these two planks, as it were, of human salvation, caring more for the business of the pen than the duty of my conscience? For since I am a sinner of all marks, and born for nothing except repentance, I cannot easily be silent about that which Adam himself too, the first of the human race and of offense against the Lord, restored to his paradise by public confession, is not silent about.

pass_b_english: If you shrink back from public confession, picture hell in your heart, which public confession will extinguish for you. First imagine the magnitude of the punishment, so that you will not hesitate to embrace the remedy. What do we think that storehouse of eternal fire is, when its mere smoke-vents stir up such eruptions of flame that nearby cities either no longer exist or expect the same fate any day? The proudest mountains burst apart from the fire conceived within them, and what proves to us the endlessness of the judgment is this: though they burst apart, though they are devoured, they are never finished. Who will not regard these torments of the mountains as previews of the threatening judgment? Who will not agree that such sparks are missiles and practice-darts from some great and immeasurable furnace? Therefore, since you know that against hell, after those first defenses of the Lord's baptism, there are still second aids in public confession, why do you abandon your salvation? Why do you hesitate to undertake what you know can heal you? Even mute and irrational creatures recognize in due time the medicines divinely assigned to them. A stag pierced by an arrow knows that it must be healed with dittany, to drive the iron and its unyielding delays from the wound. A swallow, if it has blinded its chicks, knows how to restore their sight with its own celandine. Will the sinner, knowing that public confession was established by the Lord for his restoration, pass by the very thing that restored the Babylonian king to his kingdom? For Nebuchadnezzar had long offered repentance to the Lord, performing public confession through seven years of squalor, with nails grown wild like an eagle's and neglected hair presenting a lion-like horror. What harsh treatment! The man whom humans shuddered at, God was receiving. The Egyptian ruler, by contrast, who had long persecuted God's people—once afflicted and denied to their Lord—rushed into battle, and after so many plague-signs, when the sea parted and made a way passable for God's people alone, he perished as the waves rolled back. For he had cast aside repentance and its ministry, public confession. Why should I say more about these two planks, so to speak, of human salvation? I am more concerned with the duty of my conscience than with the business of writing. For since I am a sinner of every mark, born for nothing but repentance, I cannot easily keep silent about the very thing that Adam—the originator of the human race and of offense against the Lord—does not keep silent about, having been restored to his paradise through public confession.

problems.quote: its mere smoke-vents stir up such strikes of flame
problems.why: 'Strikes of flame' is not natural English; likely means 'bursts' or 'eruptions' of flame.
problems.fix: Use 'eruptions of flame' or 'outbursts of fire.'

problems.quote: after so many proofs of plagues
problems.why: 'Proofs of plagues' is awkward; likely means 'demonstrations through plagues' or 'plague-signs.'
problems.fix: Use 'after so many plague-signs' or 'after so many plagues had been demonstrated.'
